name: Pride

counsel.text: Be much in thoughts of this nature, to abase the pride of thy heart, and to keep thy soul humble within thee. There is nothing will render thee a greater indisposition to be imposed on by the deceits of sin than such a frame of heart. Think greatly of the greatness of God.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 12

counsel.text: Oh look on Christ, this rare pattern, and be humbled! It is an unseemly sight to see God humbling himself and man exalting himself; to see a humble Saviour and a proud sinner.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: A Body of Divinity, Christ's humiliation in his incarnation

counsel.text: He that changes pride for worldliness, sensuality for Pharisaism, vanity in himself to the contempt of others, let him not think that he hath mortified the sin that he seems to have left. He hath changed his master, but is a servant still.
counsel.author: John Owen
counsel.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 5

counsel.text: Hast thou skill and parts? Be humble. Lucifer has more knowledge than thou. Hast thou grace? Be humble. Thou hast it not of thy own growth; it is borrowed. Were it not folly to be proud of a ring that is lent?
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: A Body of Divinity, Christ's humiliation in his incarnation

counsel.text: Hezekiah had the root of pride in him always; yet it did not make him run up and down to show his treasure and his riches until he fell into temptation by the ambassadors of the king of Babylon.
counsel.author: John Owen

counsel.text: A proud man sets an high value upon himself; and is angry with others, because they will not come up to his price: take heed of pride! O had others a window to look into their breast, as Crates once expressed it, or did thy heart stand where thy face doth, thou wouldst wonder to have so much respect.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Art of Divine Contentment, ch. 10

counsel.text: Let us search for the leaven of pride. This sours our holy things. Will a humble Christ be received into a proud heart? Pride keeps Christ out.
counsel.author: Thomas Watson
counsel.source: The Ten Commandments, the Lord's Supper

counsel.text: Christ came down from heaven, and emptied himself of majesty in tender love to souls; shall we not come down from our high conceits to do any poor soul good? shall man be proud after God hath been humble?
counsel.author: Richard Sibbes

counsel.text: The more we see and grieve for pride, which is an immediate issue of our corrupted nature, the less it is, because we see it by a contrary grace; the more sight the more hatred, the more hatred of sin, the more love of grace, and the more love the more life, which the more lively it is, the more it is sensible of the contrary. Upon every discovery and conflict corruption loses some ground, and grace gains upon it.
counsel.author: Richard Sibbes
counsel.source: The Soul's Conflict with Itself, ch. 12

counsel.text: A man may be very zealous in prayer, and painful in preaching, and all the while pride is the master whom he serves, though in God's livery. It can take sanctuary in the holiest actions, and hide itself under the skirt of virtue itself. Thus while a man is exercising his charity, pride may be the idol in secret for which he lavisheth out his gold so freely.
counsel.author: William Gurnall

counsel.text: Pride would be somebody, and therefore comes abroad to court the multitude; whereas humility delights in privacy. As the leaves do cover and shade the fruits, that some hand may gently lift up them, before they can see the fruit; so should a humility and holy modesty conceal the perfections of the soul, till a hand of providence by some call invites them out.
counsel.author: William Gurnall

counsel.text: Humility will make a man have high thoughts of others and low thoughts of a man's self; it will make a man see much glory and excellency in others, and much baseness and sinfulness in a man's self; it will make a man see others rich, and himself poor; others strong, and himself weak; others wise, and himself foolish.
counsel.author: Thomas Brooks

prayers.title: A prayer of confession
prayers.opening: Most holy God, high and lifted up, great and greatly to be praised, you dwell in the high and holy place, and also with the one who is contrite and lowly in spirit; I come to you only in the name of your Son.
prayers.text: I confess that I have been proud. I have sought my own glory and the praise of others. I have looked down on others in my heart, and I have taken credit for gifts that were yours to give. What do I have that I did not receive? Yet I have boasted as if I had not received it. Pride is the root under so many of my sins, and it sets me against you, for you oppose the proud. I have no excuse. But you set forth Christ as the atoning sacrifice for sin. He humbled himself to death on a cross for proud sinners, and he lives to intercede for me. For his sake, forgive me. By your Holy Spirit, put this pride to death at its root. Teach me to count others more significant than myself, to be glad when they are honored, and to be content to be unseen.
prayers.closing: I thank you that you give grace to the humble, and that this grace is mine in Christ. Not to me, O Lord, not to me, but to your name be the glory, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

prayers.title: When pride lifts its head
prayers.opening: Lord Jesus, King of glory, you humbled yourself for me, even to death on a cross.
prayers.text: You are gentle and lowly in heart, and I feel my heart lifting itself up even now. I want to be noticed, admired, and proved right. Bring me low before I fall, for pride goes before destruction. Remind me that I have nothing I did not receive from you. Let me boast only in your cross, by which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world. Holy Spirit, put this pride to death, and clothe me with humility before God and before the people in front of me.
prayers.closing: To you be all the glory, now and for ever. Amen.

prayers.title: For a lowly heart
prayers.opening: Father, you are high and lifted up, and I am dust and ashes before you; yet you look with favor on the one who is humble and trembles at your word.
prayers.text: Make me that one. Turn my eyes from myself to your majesty and your grace. Keep me from despising anyone, even in my thoughts. Make me glad when others are honored and quiet when I am overlooked. Make me like your Son, who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death. Let me serve gladly in his name, and give you all the glory.
prayers.closing: Through Jesus Christ, who emptied himself for me, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

prayers.title: Confessing the pride of our hearts
prayers.opening: Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable.
prayers.text: We have all reason to be humbled for the pride of our hearts, that we have thought of ourselves above what hath been meet, and have not thought soberly, nor walked humbly with our God. We have leaned to our own understanding, and trusted in our own hearts; and have sacrificed to our own net. We have sought our own glory more than the glory of him that sent us; and have been puffed up for that for which we should have mourned.
prayers.closing: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
prayers.author: Matthew Henry
prayers.source: arranged from A Method for Prayer, chs. 1, 2 and 7

prayers.title: For humility and meekness
prayers.opening: Thou hast appointed us a great High Priest, in whose name we may come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may find mercy and grace to help in time of need.
prayers.text: Lord, give us all to learn of Christ to be meek and lowly in heart, that we may find rest to our souls; and that herein the same mind may be in us that was also in Christ Jesus. Lord, hide pride from us, and clothe us with humility, and put upon us the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which in thy sight is of great price. Lord, give us grace to walk worthy of the vocation wherewith we are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with long-suffering forbearing one another in love.
prayers.closing: Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
prayers.author: Matthew Henry
prayers.source: arranged from A Method for Prayer, chs. 1, 3 and 7

examinationQuestions: Where today did you most want to be noticed, praised, or proved right, and what does that show you about whose glory you were living for?
What gift, success, or good name did you hold today as if it were your own, forgetting that you received it from God?
Did you look down on anyone today, in thought or in word? What would it look like to count that person more important than yourself?
How did you take correction, criticism, or being passed over? Did you resent it, or receive it as from the hand of God?
When did you last think long and quietly about the greatness of God? How large a place does he have in your thoughts compared with yourself?
Has your pride only changed its clothes, from open boasting to quiet contempt for others, or to a show of humility that still wants to be admired?
fleeActions: Stop talking about yourself. Ask the next person you see how they are, and listen to the whole answer.
Open your Bible to Philippians 2 and read slowly how Christ humbled himself. Then do one lowly task that no one will notice or thank you for.
If you were wrong today, go to the person you wronged and say so plainly, without excuses.
Speak well of someone to another person today, and mean it, especially someone you are tempted to compete with.
Kneel and thank God by name for each gift you are proud of, owning that every one came from his hand.
Ask a faithful believer in your church, or one of your elders, to tell you honestly where they see pride in you. Thank them, and do not defend yourself.

afterFallReadings.text: I have also, while found in this blessed work of Christ, been often tempted to pride and liftings up of heart; and though I dare not say I have not been infected with this, yet truly the Lord, of His precious mercy, hath so carried it towards me, that, for the most part, I have had but small joy to give way to such a thing; for it hath been my every day's portion to be let into the evil of my own heart, and still made to see such a multitude of corruptions and infirmities therein, that it hath caused hanging down of the head under all my gifts and attainments; I have felt this thorn in the flesh, the very mercy of God to me (2 Cor. 12:7-9).
afterFallReadings.author: John Bunyan
afterFallReadings.source: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, §296

afterFallReadings.text: Consider his mercifulness, tenderness, and kindness, as he is our great High Priest at the right hand of God. Assuredly he pities thee in thy distress; saith he, "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you," Isa. 66:13. He hath the tenderness of a mother to a sucking child.
afterFallReadings.author: John Owen
afterFallReadings.source: Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers, ch. 14
